Figure 1:Overview of the RSI Process and Trustworthiness Framework.The numbered labels (§2–§8) indicate the corresponding sections of this survey.
The central panel (Section 2) presents the definition and four-stage improvement cycle of RSI (S1–S4), including recursive revision and reuse of the bias update function (RI).
Four surrounding trustworthiness themes are organized under three complementary analytical roles: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight.
Section 7 examines evaluation designs and evidence requirements at the individual-update, successor, and meta-improvement levels, while §8 covers representative applications and open research problems.

Figure 2:A taxonomy roadmap of representative work on trustworthy RSI.The four themes follow Sections3–6, with shared chronological columns. Each institutional mark identifies a selected author affiliation, rather than all collaborators. The selection spans risks, limitations, safeguards, and enabling methods at different levels of improvement; inclusion does not imply demonstrated strict RI or durable protection. Arrows indicate time, not causal influence.

Figure 4:Genuine and Sustained Improvement Across S1–S4 and RI in the Process of RSI.Stage-specific risks and checks address biased diagnosis, shortcut search, misleading acceptance scores, and ineffective updates. The lower panel compares the gains, retention, and transfer of later updates produced by the original and revised improvement mechanisms, starting from matched initial states under common tests and resource budgets.

Figure 5:Behavioral Constraints, Alignment, and Fairness Across S1–S4 and RI in the Process of RSI.Behavioral requirements, authorized human goals, and fairness criteria apply throughout the four improvement stages. Each stage pairs a potential failure with a corresponding safeguard. The lower panel examines whether changes to the improvement mechanism remain authorized and whether later successors continue to satisfy the applicable behavioral, alignment, and fairness requirements.

header: 5System Security, Resilience, Privacy, and Data Governance

images.caption: Figure 6:System Security, Resilience, Privacy, and Data Governance Across S1–S4 and RI in the Process of RSI.The two rows distinguish security and resilience from privacy and data governance. Stage-specific risks and safeguards cover compromised experience, malicious or sensitive derived assets, unreliable admission evidence, and inherited threats or information exposure. The lower panel outlines independent approval, renewed protection checks, and tests of successors after the improvement mechanism is revised and reused.

Figure 7:Transparency and Controllability Across S1–S4 and RI in the Process of RSI.The four stages connect testable diagnoses, proposed interventions, independent evaluation, and enforceable correction. Cross-stage oversight requires testable explanations, traceable sources and revisions, and independent review. Authorized interventions must reach affected inherited components and active processes, while separate tests establish their actual effects. The lower panel extends these checks to monitoring and control after improvement-mechanism revision and reuse.

Figure 9:Three-level comparison design for longitudinal RSI evaluation.Update-level comparisons separate development, acceptance, and independent
reporting after S4; successor-level comparisons track inherited outcomes
across versions; and meta-improvement comparisons use paired continuations
with fixed updaters. All three assess task performance, constraint
satisfaction, and oversight effectiveness.
